title: SOC triage: alerts, phishing, threat intel and AI verdicts
summary: Work a ten-alert morning queue at a lake-side hotel group: triage five reported emails, write and test a YARA rule, check indicators against intel and map them to ATT&CK, decode a suspicious command in CyberChef, and review an AI assistant's verdicts, including one that obeyed text an attacker wrote.
titlePrefix: SOC triage: alerts, phishing, threat intel and AI verdicts
rubric: Ten dispositions, each with a one-line reason a stranger could check
Exactly one escalation, written with the ask first
Phishing report: sender, authentication results, the real link, pressure tactics and a verdict for each email
YARA rule that matches the lure and not the intel feed or logs, with its test result
Intel note: indicators checked against the feed, defanged, mapped to ATT&CK
AI-verdict review log: every verdict agreed or overridden, each override backed by evidence, including the alert that carried text written for the AI
Plain writing: facts kept apart from guesses
handin: Ten dispositions with one escalation, a phishing report with a tested YARA rule, an intel note, and an AI-verdict review log.

script.intro: Welcome to SOC triage. Lotus Lake Hotels runs three lake-side hotels in Udaipur, and it's Wednesday the eleventh of November, the first busy week of the wedding season. Bookings are flowing, advances are being paid to decorators and caterers, and staff are pressing the Report phishing button on everything that looks odd. You're the analyst on the morning shift, and you have ten alerts. Triage means sorting: closing what's noise, recording what's already been dealt with, and finding the one thing that needs a person to act now. Today we'll learn how the alert queue works, triage five reported emails from their headers, work the whole queue, decode a suspicious command in CyberChef, write and test a YARA rule, check indicators against threat intelligence and map them to ATT&CK, and review the verdicts of an AI assistant, including one that was fooled by words an attacker wrote. Only one alert deserves an escalation. Let's find it.

steps.say: Step one: how the alert queue works. An alert queue is the program a SOC analyst lives in. It collects alerts from the mail gateway, the web proxy, antivirus, sign-in logs and staff reports, and lines them up for a person to decide. The Linux cell shows the raw file behind the queue: it's just JSON. Then we open the same file in the queue, without deciding anything yet, and look around.
steps.after: Every alert has the same fields: an ID, a time, the rule that fired, the host and user it's about, a detail line, a severity from the system that raised it, and an evidence list, the files to open next. The queue never decides. You give each alert one of five dispositions. True positive, escalate: real, and a person must act now. True positive, handled: real, but already contained, blocked, removed or quarantined. Benign: the rule worked, but what it saw is normal here. False positive: the rule matched something it was never meant to catch. And needs more information, which is only allowed if you write the question and who can answer it. The difference between handled and benign is whether anything bad happened. A blocked phishing click is handled. A scanner doing its job is benign. Notice too that the queue sorts by severity, which the source systems set, not you. High doesn't mean urgent, and low doesn't mean safe. Answer the questions: evidence, and five.

steps.say: Step two: read the morning queue. Before deciding anything, read every alert once, end to end, and hash the evidence, so you can show later that nothing changed while you worked. Look for groups: which alerts are reported emails, and which come from machines. And look for money and a deadline.
steps.after: Ten alerts. Five are emails that staff reported or forwarded, from Reservations, Accounts and Housekeeping. The other five come from machines: an encoded PowerShell command on the booking server, a sign-in from a new country, antivirus quarantining a file at the front desk, a port scan, and a DMARC report. And one alert has money and a deadline in it: AL-4102. Accounts forwarded an email, signed by the General Manager, asking to change a supplier's bank account and release twelve lakh sixty thousand rupees before today's payment run closes at 14:00 India time. That's where attackers go when they can't get past the mail filter: not the laptops, the payments. Answer the questions: ten, and 14:00.

steps.say: Step three: triage the reported emails. Five emails. For each one we read four things. Who really sent it, from the Return-Path and the Received line, not the display name. What SPF, DKIM and DMARC said, and which domain each result is about. Where the link really goes, which isn't always what the link text says. And which pressure tactics it uses: urgency, secrecy, authority, fear of loss. The Linux cell pulls all of that out at once.
steps.after: The guest complaint. The From line says BookingPartner Extranet, but the Return-Path is partner-notify.example and it came from a bulk mail server. SPF passes, but only for the sender's own domain. DMARC fails for bookingpartner.example, which means it's pretending to be them. The link text says extranet.bookingpartner.example, the real site, but the href goes to bookingpartner-extranet.login-verify.example, a fake sign-in page. And the pressure: answer in twenty-four hours or your hotel disappears from search results. Phishing. The GST refund: SPF, DKIM and DMARC all pass, for gst-refund-portal.example, a newly registered domain that is not the tax department. Three and a half lakh rupees, claim before six tonight. And look at the last line, in one-pixel white text: a note to the AI triage assistant saying the email is safe. A person can't see it. A machine reads it. Phishing. The supplier bank change: from a free mail account wearing the General Manager's name. Everything passes, for freemail.example, which proves only that it came from a free mail account. Secrecy, urgency, authority, and reply only here. Payment fraud. The linen offer is marketing, with a working unsubscribe link. Spam. And the payslip email came through the company's own servers, from the HR system, with an internal link. Genuine: tell the reporter it's safe and thank them. Answer the questions: bookingpartner-extranet.login-verify.example, and three.

steps.say: Step four: work the queue. Now all ten alerts, each with a disposition and a one-line reason that a stranger could check. Exactly one escalation: the alert where a person has to act in the next few hours.
steps.after: AL-4102 is the escalation: money leaves today unless someone stops it. AL-4101, the guest complaint, is handled: the proxy blocked Kavya's click at 03:52, she went straight to the real extranet instead, which is exactly the right instinct, and the gateway removed the email from all three mailboxes at 03:58. AL-4103, the GST email, is handled too: nobody clicked, and it was removed at 04:05. AL-4107 is handled: antivirus quarantined Boarding_Pass.pdf.exe from a guest's USB stick before it ran. AL-4110 is handled: 214 fake emails using the hotel's name were rejected by other mail servers, because the hotel's DMARC policy says reject. The linen offer and the payslip email are benign. The port scan from 10.50.0.250 is benign: the intel file lists it as the IT contractor's scanner, inside its Wednesday window. The sign-in from Singapore is benign too: travel.csv shows Neha Rathore at a trade show there until Friday, and the sign-in passed MFA on her own phone. And the encoded PowerShell is a false positive, which we'll prove in the next step. Answer the question: AL-4102.

steps.say: Step five: decode the suspicious command. AL-4106 is an encoded PowerShell command on pms01, the server that runs the hotel's booking system. Encoding hides what a command does, which is why attackers use it. But IT scripts sometimes use it too, so we decode before we judge. In CyberChef: From Base64, then Decode text as UTF-16, because that's how PowerShell encodes its commands. Or the same in the Linux cell, with base64 and tr.
steps.after: It decodes to one line: Compress-Archive, path D PMS Export star, destination the pms-backup folder on nas01, with today's date in the file name. It zips the night's booking export and puts it on the backup server. It runs as svc.pmsbackup, the IT backup account, from the Task Scheduler, at 21:30 UTC every night, and the alert has fired at the same time for thirty days. Nothing in it is harmful. So it's a false positive: the rule fires on any encoded PowerShell, and this script was never what it was meant to catch. The disposition alone isn't enough, though. Write a note to IT: please rewrite the scheduled task without encoding, or give us the task, account and host so we can add a narrow exception. Otherwise this alert fires every night, and one night somebody stops reading it. Answer the question: Compress-Archive.

steps.say: Step six: a YARA rule for the lure. YARA describes a file by the strings inside it, and the mail gateway can use YARA rules to catch the next copy of a phishing email. We test every rule on every file in the case. The first rule matches on the phishing domain alone. Let's see what else it catches.
steps.after: Five files match: the alert queue, the intel feed, the hotel association's block list, the proxy log, and the email itself. Only one of those is an email. A rule like that, on the mail gateway, would be harmless, but on a file share or in an analyst's notes it would fire all day. The tuned rule needs three things together that only the lure has: a subject starting Guest complaint BKG, a link to login-verify.example slash complaints, and the threat, hidden from search results. It matches one file, guest-complaint.eml. The third rule shows how YARA is usually used: on malware. It describes the stealer from the guest's USB stick by four strings, its mutex, the path to Chrome's saved passwords, its grab-all flag and the address it sends stolen files to, and it needs three of the four. One match. Under each rule, write what it would miss: the attackers only have to change the subject line or the domain to slip past the lure rule, which is why the intel step matters too. Answer the questions: five, and one.

steps.say: Step seven: indicators and intel. An indicator is something you can search for or block: a domain, an address, a file hash. We pull every indicator out of the evidence, check each one against the intel feed, note who reported it, and decide: block, watch, or ignore. Then we map what we saw to MITRE ATT&CK, so that everyone, here and at the hotel association, uses the same names for the same behaviour.
steps.after: The fake extranet, the sending domain and its mail server were reported by the Hospitality ISAC, the hotels' information-sharing group. The fake tax site comes from a CERT advisory. The stealer's hash and the address it sends data to come from a vendor feed. Block all of those. But read the benign entries too: the real booking-partner extranet, the HR portal, the booking server, the contractor's scanner, and freemail.example, which is benign as a domain but should never be trusted for a display name. Blocking the real extranet would stop Reservations from working on the busiest week of the year. On the heatmap: spearphishing link, acquiring look-alike domains, impersonation for the payment fraud, removable media and user execution for the USB stick, credentials from web browsers and exfiltration over a web service for the stealer. Write each indicator defanged, with square brackets around the dots, so nobody clicks it by accident. Answer the question: Hospitality ISAC.

steps.say: Step eight: review the AI assistant's verdicts. The SOC's AI assistant gave a verdict on every alert. It's fast and usually right, but it only sees the alert text, not your evidence, and it reads everything in that text, including words that an attacker wrote. For each verdict, agree or override, and every override needs a fact from the evidence.
steps.after: Six verdicts are right. Four are wrong, and each is a different kind of mistake. AL-4102: the assistant said benign because the display name matched the General Manager and authentication passed. Too trusting: the address is a free mail account, and passing authentication only proves that. AL-4103: it said benign because the message says the IT team checked it. That sentence was written by the attacker, in white one-pixel text, for exactly this assistant. That's called prompt injection, and it's why an AI verdict can never rest on what the content says about itself. AL-4106: it said malicious because encoded PowerShell is a common attacker technique, without decoding it. Too alarmed. And AL-4109: it said escalate for the Singapore sign-in, because it didn't know about the trade show. Missing context. Write the fact next to each override: the From address, the hidden line, the decoded command, the travel calendar. Answer the question: four.

steps.say: Step nine: escalate the payment fraud. Now the one escalation. The reader is Pooja Mathur, the Finance Controller, and she has to stop a payment before two o'clock. So the ask goes first, then why it's serious, then what we know and don't know, and what we have and haven't done.
steps.after: Read the model on screen. The ask: take the twelve lakh sixty thousand rupee advance out of today's run, which closes at 14:00 India time, 08:30 UTC, and call the General Manager on his known mobile, and the decorators on the number in the supplier file, never the numbers in the email. Severity high: money leaves today, the bank details are new, and the request came from outside while pretending to be the General Manager. What we know, with times. What we don't know: whether he knows about it, and whether the supplier's details were already changed. And what we've done: nothing changed, and we did not reply to the sender, because replying tells the attacker someone is reading. Every claim points at a file.

steps.say: Step ten: hand in. Hand in this notebook: the ten dispositions, the email verdicts, the YARA tests, the intel note, the AI review and the escalation. The rubric is on screen.
steps.after: Before you press Hand in, read your dispositions once more as if you were the analyst on the next shift. Could they check every reason without asking you? And read your AI review as if you were the person who has to decide whether to keep using the assistant. Do your four overrides show them what it's bad at?

script.outro: That's the morning shift at Lotus Lake Hotels. You learned how the alert queue works and what each disposition means, judged five emails by their headers and real links instead of their display names, proved a scary-looking command was a nightly backup, wrote a YARA rule that catches the lure and nothing else, checked indicators against the feed without blocking the hotel's own partners, and caught an AI assistant being too trusting, too alarmed, missing context, and obeying a sentence written for it by an attacker. And you found the one alert that mattered: a payment, a deadline and a fake General Manager. Next is Capstone A, where you run a whole night shift on your own. Thank you for watching.

# SOC triage: alerts, phishing, threat intel and AI verdicts (Practice)

Practice: the same Wednesday queue at Lotus Lake Hotels, with fewer hints and harder questions. Many answers need a time converted between UTC and IST, or two files read together.

The files for this seminar are in `~/case` (Linux) and `case/` (Python): `ai-verdicts.json`, `alerts-wednesday.json`, `intel.json`, `known_bad.txt`, `mail.log`, `proxy.log`, `README.txt`, `reported/gst-refund.eml`, `reported/guest-complaint.eml`, `reported/linen-offer.eml`, `reported/payslips.eml`, `reported/supplier-bank-change.eml`, `suspect/boarding-pass.strings.txt`, `travel.csv`.

## 1. How the alert queue works

Before you triage, learn the program. An alert queue (the triage console of a SOC) takes alerts from many sources, the mail gateway, the proxy, antivirus, sign-in logs and staff who press **Report phishing**, and lines them up for a person to decide.

Every alert carries the same fields: an **ID**, the **time**, the **rule** that fired, the **host** and **user** it is about, a **detail** line, and the **evidence** files to open next. The queue doesn't decide anything. You give each alert one **disposition**:

| Disposition | Meaning |
|---|---|
| True positive: escalate | Real, and a person must act now |
| True positive: handled | Real, and already contained (blocked, removed, quarantined) |
| Benign: expected activity | The rule worked, but what it saw is normal here |
| False positive: rule fired wrongly | The rule matched something it was never meant to catch |
| Needs more information | You can't decide yet: write the question and who can answer it |

The Linux cell shows the raw queue file, so you can see that the program is only reading JSON. The queue below is the one you will work today, at **Lotus Lake Hotels** in Udaipur. Don't set any dispositions yet: just open it and look around. Read `README.txt` first.

- [ ] Compare the raw JSON with how the queue shows the same alert
- [ ] Open one alert's evidence list
- [ ] Find the summary line that counts dispositions

```tool alerts
{"file": "alerts-wednesday.json", "d": "", "n": 0, "blank": ["d"], "a": {"d": {}}}
```

?> How many alerts in the queue have severity high? :: sha256:4e07408562bedb8b60ce05c1decfe3ad16b72230967de01f640b7e4729b49fce

# Your turn. Write the code for this step, then press Run.
# Hint: the recording started with head.
template.a:
cd ~/case
head -c 700 alerts-wednesday.json; echo
grep -c '"id"' alerts-wednesday.json

## 2. Read the morning queue

It's Wednesday 11 November, the first busy week of the wedding season at Lotus Lake Hotels. Hotels are a favourite target at this time of year: bookings, advances to suppliers and guests' cards all move fast. You have ten alerts. Your job is to close what is noise, finish what is already handled, and escalate only what needs a person now.

Read the queue once end to end before you decide anything. Then hash the evidence, so you can show later that nothing changed while you worked.

- [ ] Hash every evidence file
- [ ] Read all ten alerts
- [ ] Which alerts are reported emails, and which come from machines?
- [ ] Which one has money and a deadline today?

?> How many rupees are at risk in AL-4102? (digits only) :: sha256:de21a458042f4d851f1b484c49fd7c526428047e4f8c21fd042c24122cbd86ae

?> AL-4102 reached the SOC at 04:20 UTC. How many minutes were left before the payment run closed? :: sha256:1e472b39b105d349bcd069c4a711b44a2fffb8e274714bb07ecfff69a9a7f67b

# Your turn. Write the code for this step, then press Run.
# Hint: the recording started with sha256sum.
template.a:
cd ~/case
sha256sum *.* reported/* suspect/*
echo ---
grep -E '"(id|rule|host)"' alerts-wednesday.json

## 3. Triage the reported emails

Five emails were reported. For each one, read who **really** sent it (Return-Path and the Received line), what SPF, DKIM and DMARC said, where the link **really** goes, and which pressure tactics it uses. Then give a verdict: phishing, payment fraud (BEC), spam, or genuine.

- [ ] Sender, Reply-To and Return-Path for each email
- [ ] Authentication results, and which domain each result is about
- [ ] The real link target, not the link text
- [ ] Pressure tactics: urgency, secrecy, authority, fear of loss
- [ ] Anything in the email that isn't meant for a human reader
- [ ] A verdict for each

```tool email
{"d": "", "n": 3, "files": ["reported/guest-complaint.eml", "reported/gst-refund.eml", "reported/linen-offer.eml", "reported/payslips.eml", "reported/supplier-bank-change.eml"], "blank": ["d"], "a": {"d": {"reported/guest-complaint.eml": "phish", "reported/gst-refund.eml": "phish", "reported/linen-offer.eml": "spam", "reported/payslips.eml": "legit", "reported/supplier-bank-change.eml": "bec"}}}
```

?> Which IP address delivered the guest-complaint email? :: sha256:a6353bfbe92ae34a8544b367820743d0175595f96dcad8b904c39583f24c3eec

?> At what UTC time (HH:MM:SS) did the proxy block k.bhati's click? :: sha256:d533fbda5835f1303dfaf24ba8694149a8de379e336211a4e3a3a257b741cb29

?> How many seconds later did the same PC open the real booking-partner extranet? :: sha256:6f4b6612125fb3a0daecd2799dfd6c9c299424fd920f9b308110a2c1fbd8f443

# Your turn. Write the code for this step, then press Run.
# Hint: the recording started with grep.
template.a:
cd ~/case/reported
grep -H -E '^(From|Reply-To|Return-Path):' *.eml
echo ---
grep -H -o 'spf=[a-z]*\|dkim=[a-z]*\|dmarc=[a-z]*' *.eml
echo ---
grep -H -o 'href="[^"]*"' *.eml
echo ---
grep -H 'font-size:1px' *.eml

## 4. Work the queue

Now give all ten alerts a disposition and a one-line reason. **Exactly one** should be escalated: the one where a person must act in the next few hours. Already-contained activity is "true positive: handled". Normal activity that a rule noticed is "benign". A rule that fired on something it was never meant to catch is "false positive".

- [ ] Every alert has a disposition
- [ ] One escalation
- [ ] Each reason points at evidence (a log line, a header, a file)
- [ ] Write the notes for the next shift

```tool alerts
{"file": "alerts-wednesday.json", "d": "", "n": 1, "blank": ["d"], "a": {"d": {"AL-4101": "handled", "AL-4102": "escalate", "AL-4103": "handled", "AL-4104": "benign", "AL-4105": "benign", "AL-4106": "false", "AL-4107": "handled", "AL-4108": "benign", "AL-4109": "benign", "AL-4110": "handled"}}}
```

?> Who approved Neha Rathore's trip? :: sha256:f0b56fd2994a1c4543284f4129ac5920f8ffdc5626110812d67b37da2a373da0

?> Did AL-4108 fire inside the scanner's scheduled window? (yes or no) :: sha256:8a798890fe93817163b10b5f7bd2ca4d25d84c52739a645a889c173eee7d9d3d

## 5. Decode the suspicious command

AL-4106 is an encoded PowerShell command on pms01, the server that runs the hotel's booking system. Encoding hides what a command does, which is why attackers use it, but IT scripts sometimes use it too. Decode it before you judge it.

[Open the command in CyberChef](https://zeffiroh.github.io/ap-cybersecurity/cyberchef/#recipe=From_Base64%28%27A-Za-z0-9%252B/%253D%27,true,false%29Decode_text%28%27UTF-16LE%2520%281200%29%27%29&) (From Base64, then Decode text as UTF-16LE). Or decode it in the Linux cell.

- [ ] Decode the command
- [ ] What does it do? Is anything in it harmful?
- [ ] Which account runs it, and when?
- [ ] Write the disposition and a note to IT: an encoded command in a scheduled task trips the alert every night

?> To which server does the backup zip go? (server name) :: sha256:8ec0bfadaccf670e37cb70a773f3822cdaaf2f2d62621808a29595a913966f96

?> On how many days in a row has AL-4106 fired? :: sha256:624b60c58c9d8bfb6ff1886c2fd605d2adeb6ea4da576068201b6c6958ce93f4

# Your turn. Write the code for this step, then press Run.
# Hint: the recording started with echo.

## 6. A YARA rule for the lure

Write a YARA rule that finds the guest-complaint lure in mail, so the mail gateway can catch the next one. Test it on **every** file. The first rule below matches on the phishing domain alone: see what else it catches. The tuned rule needs three things that only the lure email has.

- [ ] Test the noisy rule: which files does it match? Are they emails?
- [ ] Test the tuned rule: it should match only guest-complaint.eml
- [ ] Test the third rule on the quarantined file's strings
- [ ] Write one line on what each rule would miss

```tool yara
{"rule": "", "n": 5, "files": ["alerts-wednesday.json", "ai-verdicts.json", "intel.json", "known_bad.txt", "mail.log", "proxy.log", "reported/guest-complaint.eml"], "blank": ["rule"], "a": {"rule": "rule llh_phishing_domain
{
  meta:
    description = "Anything that mentions the phishing domain"
  strings:
    $d = "login-verify.example"
  condition:
    $d
}
"}}
```

```tool yara
{"rule": "", "n": 1, "files": ["reported/guest-complaint.eml"], "blank": ["rule"], "a": {"rule": "rule llh_guest_complaint_lure
{
  meta:
    description = "The fake guest-complaint email aimed at hotel reservations teams"
    author = "SOC"
    reference = "AL-4101, message 7C1A20F11"
  strings:
    $subject = "Subject: Guest complaint BKG-"
    $link = "login-verify.example/complaints/"
    $press = "hidden from search results"
  condition:
    all of them
}
"}}
```

```tool yara
{"rule": "", "n": 1, "files": ["suspect/boarding-pass.strings.txt"], "blank": ["rule"], "a": {"rule": "rule bp_grab_stealer_strings
{
  meta:
    description = "Strings from Boarding_Pass.pdf.exe, a password stealer left on guest USB sticks"
  strings:
    $mutex = "Global\\bp-grab-7731"
    $chrome = "\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\Default\\Login Data"
    $flag = "--grab-all"
    $exfil = "telegram-relay.example/bot"
  condition:
    3 of them
}
"}}
```

?> How many indicators in intel.json are marked malicious? :: sha256:e7f6c011776e8db7cd330b54174fd76f7d0216b612387a5ffcfb81e6f0919683

## 7. Indicators and intel

Pull every indicator out of the evidence, check it against the intel feed, and map what you saw to ATT&CK. Your intel note lists each indicator **defanged** (login-verify[.]example), says which source knows it, and says what to do: block, watch or ignore.

- [ ] Extract indicators
- [ ] Which are on the feed, and from which source?
- [ ] Which names and addresses must not be blocked?
- [ ] Map the three campaigns to ATT&CK: the fake booking partner, the fake GST refund and the USB stealer, plus the payment fraud
- [ ] Write the intel note

```tool ioc
{"attack": "", "blank": ["iocs", "attack"], "a": {"attack": ["T1566.002", "T1583.001", "T1656", "T1091", "T1204.002", "T1555.003", "T1567"]}}
```

?> Which source reported gst-refund-portal.example? :: sha256:d706fe2ae9d11dbb49d9a3961b955e5969d28097999af88b6ebea7c0186db6af

?> How many days before this Wednesday did the Hospitality ISAC first see the fake extranet domain? :: sha256:7902699be42c8a8e46fbbb4501726517e86b22c56a189f7625a6da49081b2451

## 8. Review the AI assistant's verdicts

The SOC's AI triage assistant gave a verdict on every alert. It is fast and usually right, but it only sees the alert text, not your evidence, and it reads **everything** in that text, including words an attacker wrote. Agree, or override it and say why. **Every override needs a fact** from the evidence.

- [ ] Read each verdict and its reason
- [ ] Agree or override
- [ ] For each override, the fact that proves it wrong
- [ ] For each override, the kind of mistake: too trusting, too alarmed, missing context, or obeying text an attacker wrote

```tool aisec
{"file": "ai-verdicts.json", "marks": "", "n": 10, "blank": ["marks"], "a": {"marks": {"AL-4101": "agree", "AL-4102": "override", "AL-4103": "override", "AL-4104": "agree", "AL-4105": "agree", "AL-4106": "override", "AL-4107": "agree", "AL-4108": "agree", "AL-4109": "override", "AL-4110": "agree"}}}
```

?> Which alert did the AI call benign because of a sentence written inside the email? :: sha256:cba17863d484748b5760a4ac1a5ae16173b6089e6af161cc41245806dd37a5a4

?> Which alert did the AI escalate that the travel calendar explains? :: sha256:b539420411f9078b8d4cbc3afadd0c1f9409f748f550bbe96f06d7d59a0be630

## 9. Escalate the payment fraud

Write the one escalation. The person reading it is the Finance Controller, Pooja Mathur, who must stop a payment before 2 pm IST. Put the ask first, and say what you have **not** done (you didn't reply to the sender).

- [ ] The ask, with a time in the reader's time zone and in UTC
- [ ] Why it is high
- [ ] Know and don't know
- [ ] Where the evidence is

```tool report
{"tpl": "escalation", "title": "Escalation: payment fraud attempt against Accounts", "text": "", "n": 7, "blank": ["text"], "a": {"text": "# Escalation: payment fraud attempt against Accounts

## The ask

Please take the Rs 12,60,000 advance to Rang Mahal Decorators out of today's payment run, which closes at 14:00 IST (08:30 UTC).
```
